records.our_prose: You can snip oregano anytime once it is established: cut the top few inches of leafy stems. The flavor is strongest just before it flowers, so that is the best time to cut oregano to dry, in the morning after the dew dries. Pinching off the flower buds keeps the leaves tasting their best, and snipping it often keeps it bushy. Oregano is unusual in that it tastes even stronger once dried.

records.our_prose: In Utah's Dixie high desert, oregano is a desert-strong perennial: common oregano is hardy well below zone 8, to about zone 4, so winter cold is not this region's real constraint. What matters here is the opposite of a humid-belt cell: this crop thrives in the heat, summer temperatures are not a problem, and established plants are genuinely drought-tolerant, and St. George's dry air and alkaline soil suit oregano's Mediterranean origin far better than a humid climate would, with none of the wet-soil rot risk that troubles it elsewhere. Give it full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, and water only infrequently once established. Establish plants in the shoulder season, spring or fall, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah.

records.our_prose: Oregano reaches the grower as several practical types. Greek oregano (Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum) is the hot, pungent kitchen standard and the type sold dried; Italian oregano (O. x majoricum, an oregano-marjoram hybrid) is milder and sweeter. Common or wild oregano (O. vulgare) is the hardiest and most vigorous but has variable, sometimes bland flavor, so taste before you rely on it. Hot & Spicy is an extra-pungent selection, Golden oregano (O. vulgare 'Aureum') is a bright-foliaged ornamental-culinary form, and Syrian oregano (O. syriacum) is the tender za'atar herb. One important caution: Mexican oregano (Lippia graveolens) is not a true oregano at all but a shrub in the verbena family, grown in hot climates for a similar, stronger flavor. For cooking, start with Greek oregano.
